chapter_title: Automating Incident Detection with CloudWatch and EventBridge

screens.title: Automating Incident Detection with CloudWatch and EventBridge
screens.subtitle: Build dynamic detectors, combine alarms, and route events to automated responders

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how to move beyond simple threshold alarms to build smarter, more reliable incident detection. We cover metric math for derived signals, anomaly detection for dynamic thresholds, and composite alarms to combine multiple signals into meaningful alerts. Then we show how EventBridge receives and routes alarm events so you can orchestrate automated responses with Lambda, Step Functions, queues, and tickets. You will see concrete CLI examples for enabling an anomaly detector and creating an alarm that uses the learned band, and a compact EventBridge rule pattern that routes state changes to a Lambda that enriches and forwards events. This matters because static thresholds lead to false positives, and one-off alarm actions limit flexibility. By the end you'll know when to use metric math versus a composite alarm, how anomaly detection reduces alert fatigue, and how EventBridge turns alarms into extensible automation. Consider what level of detection your systems need and which events deserve automated remediation.

screens.title: Metric Math — Derive meaningful signals
screens.subtitle: Use expressions to compute new time series from raw metrics

narration.text: Metric math lets you compute new time series by applying arithmetic and functions to existing CloudWatch metrics. Rather than alarming on raw counts, you can create a ratio or a normalized metric that better represents system health. For example, calculating an application error rate by dividing 5xx error count by total requests produces a signal that is stable across different traffic volumes. This definition matters because raw counts often correlate with traffic: more users cause more errors even when the rate is unchanged. A concrete example: suppose your web tier emits a metric for 5xx errors and a metric for total requests. Metric math allows you to create an expression like errors divided by requests to get error rate. A common misconception is that metric math is only for complex statistics. In practice, many useful observability signals are simple arithmetic across two or three series. When designing metric math, ensure each input uses the same period and aggregation so the derived series is meaningful. Also plan labels and alarm names carefully so downstream automations and dashboards reference the derived signal. What derived signal would best reveal a real user-facing problem in your application?

keyIdea.title: Metric math creates clearer signals
keyIdea.text: Derive ratios or normalized metrics to avoid alerting on raw volume-driven values.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Metric Math
Metric Math — Definition
Compose arithmetic expressions across metrics to produce a new time series for analysis and alarming.
Key points:
  • Ensure inputs use the same period and statistic so the expression is valid.
  • Use metric math to normalize counts into rates or percentages.
  • Label derived series clearly so dashboards and alarms point to the correct signal.
Concrete example
Compute error rate by dividing 5xx count by total requests to get a traffic-normalized view. Alarm on the resulting series rather than raw 5xx count.
Key Takeaway

Metric math reduces false alerts by deriving signals that reflect true service problems, not traffic volume.

Implementation notes
When authoring expressions in CloudWatch, use metric IDs like m1 and m2 and a final expression that returns data. ReturnData flags control which series are visible and alarmable.
Common mistake
Mixing periods or aggregations across inputs. If one metric uses 1-minute averages and another uses 5-minute sums, the derived result will be misleading. Always align period and statistic.
Check your understanding
If your total requests double but 5xx count stays the same, what happens to the error rate derived by metric math? Think about whether the alarm should fire.

screens.title: Compute Error Rate — CLI Example
screens.subtitle: Create a metric math alarm for error rate via AWS CLI

narration.text: In this walkthrough we convert two raw metrics into a usable alarm: 5xx error count and total requests. The goal is a derived time series representing error rate and an alarm that triggers when the rate exceeds a threshold. First, you define the two input metrics with the same period and statistic inside the metrics JSON. Then you add a simple expression like m1 / m2, where m1 is 5xx and m2 is requests. The returned series uses the expression's Id and becomes the alarmable metric. A common confusion is expecting the expression to alter underlying metric granularity; it does not — you must choose a period that matches your monitoring cadence. After creating the metric math alarm, test by generating traffic with controlled errors; watch the CloudWatch Metrics view to ensure the derived series behaves as expected. If the alarm fires too often, adjust the evaluation periods, period, or use anomaly detection instead. Which threshold or evaluation period would you choose for a public-facing A P I where a brief spike in errors is acceptable? Compute Error Rate — CLI Example means define inputs with consistent periods, add an expression, and alarm on the expression result to detect rate-based issues.. In practical terms, create a metric math alarm for error rate via aws cli. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Practical CLI creation
keyIdea.text: Define inputs with consistent periods, add an expression, and alarm on the expression result to detect rate-based issues.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Error Rate — CLI
Code walkthrough
An example AWS CLI call to create an alarm with metric math. Use consistent period and statistic for inputs.
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "ErrorRate-Alarm" \
  --metric-name "ErrorRateDerived" \
  --namespace "Custom/MyApp" \
  --period 60 \
  --evaluation-periods 2 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --threshold 0.05 \
  --metrics '[{"Id":"m1","MetricStat":{"Metric":{"Namespace":"Custom/MyApp","MetricName":"5xxCount"},"Period":60,"Stat":"Sum"},"ReturnData":false},{"Id":"m2","MetricStat":{"Metric":{"Namespace":"Custom/MyApp","MetricName":"RequestCount"},"Period":60,"Stat":"Sum"},"ReturnData":false},{"Id":"e1","Expression":"m1/m2","Label":"ErrorRate","ReturnData":true}]' \
  --alarm-actions
Replace the topic ARN and ensure both metrics are emitted at the chosen period. Use ReturnData flags to control which series appear in graphs and which are used for alarms.
Supporting notes
  • Choose period based on expected reaction time and metric emission cadence.
  • Set evaluation periods to avoid transient spikes triggering alarms.
  • Label the expression clearly for dashboards and automation references.
Analogy
Think of metric math as a calculator that turns raw sensor readings into an index you can watch, like turning temperature and humidity into a comfort index.
Pro Tip

If your inputs sometimes have missing data, set the alarm's treat-missing-data flag to avoid unintended firing.

screens.title: Anomaly Detection — Adaptive thresholds
screens.subtitle: Let CloudWatch learn a metric's normal band and alert on deviations

narration.text: Anomaly detection uses CloudWatch machine learning to model normal behavior for a metric and surface values that fall outside that learned band. You enable an anomaly detector on a metric, CloudWatch observes historical data for a few days, and then it provides an expected upper and lower threshold. This is ideal for metrics with regular cycles — daily traffic peaks or weekly batch jobs — where static thresholds cause false positives. A concrete example: network egress that spikes every afternoon due to a feed would cause a static threshold alarm to ring daily; an anomaly detector learns that pattern and only alerts when the metric departs from expected behavior. A common misconception is that anomaly detection eliminates the need for human thresholds entirely; it does not. You should review the learned model, adjust the sensitivity, and use anomaly detection alongside business-aware rules. Also consider evaluation periods and treat-missing-data settings because the model needs consistent historical samples to be reliable. How would you evaluate whether an anomaly detector's sensitivity is appropriate for a production service? Anomaly Detection — Adaptive thresholds means anomaly detection adapts thresholds to normal patterns so alerts occur only when behavior meaningfully deviates.. In practical terms, let cloudwatch learn a metric's normal band and alert on deviations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Dynamic baselines reduce false positives
keyIdea.text: Anomaly detection adapts thresholds to normal patterns so alerts occur only when behavior meaningfully deviates.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Anomaly Detection
What is Anomaly Detection?
A machine-learned model creates expected upper and lower bounds for a metric given historical patterns and seasonality.
Practical notes:
  • Good for metrics without clear static thresholds.
  • Allows dynamic thresholds that account for daily and weekly cycles.
  • Model requires several days of history to become reliable.
Example

Enable an anomaly detector on EC2 CPUUtilization and create an alarm that fires when CPU is outside the learned band. This prevents constant alerts during predictable peak periods.

Common mistakes
  • Turning on anomaly detection and immediately expecting instant alerts — model requires training.
  • Using anomaly detection for highly erratic metrics with no pattern — it may not learn a stable baseline.
Check your understanding
If a metric exhibits strong weekly patterns, why is anomaly detection usually better than a static threshold? Consider both false positives and missed detections.

screens.title: Enable Anomaly Detector — Step-by-step
screens.subtitle: CLI commands and expectations for training and alarms

narration.text: This step-by-step shows the commands and the behavior you should expect after enabling anomaly detection. First, use the CLI to create an anomaly detector for the metric and statistic combination. CloudWatch then collects historical data; this training period may take several days depending on the metric cadence. After training, create a metric alarm that uses the anomaly detector by referencing the detector via a threshold-metric-id and an expression like ANOMALY_DETECTION_BAND(m1). One frequent source of confusion is the threshold-metric-id parameter: it links the alarm to the detector and the metrics block must include both the underlying metric and the anomaly expression. In practice, after you create the alarm generate a controlled load to verify the alarm enters ALARM state only when the metric leaves the expected band. Use the console's metric visual to inspect the learned band and evaluate sensitivity. When testing, allow time for the detector to warm up and avoid short transient tests that produce inconclusive results. Enable Anomaly Detector — Step-by-step means enable the detector, allow it to learn, then create an alarm that references the learned band and verify with realistic load.. In practical terms, cli commands and expectations for training and alarms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Create, wait, test
keyIdea.text: Enable the detector, allow it to learn, then create an alarm that references the learned band and verify with realistic load.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Enable Anomaly Detector
Step-by-step
Commands to create a detector and an alarm that uses the learned band.
# Create anomaly detector for EC2 CPU
aws cloudwatch put-anomaly-detector \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --stat "Average" \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=

# Create alarm referencing anomaly detector
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm \
  --alarm-name "CPU-Anomaly-Alarm" \
  --alarm-description "Alarm when CPU is outside anomaly band" \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization \
  --namespace AWS/EC2 \
  --statistic Average \
  --period 300 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanUpperThreshold \
  --threshold-metric-id ad1 \
  --metrics '[{"Id":"m1","MetricStat": {"Metric": {"Namespace":"AWS/EC2","MetricName":"CPUUtilization","Dimensions":[{"Name":"InstanceId","Value":""}]},"Period":300,"Stat":"Average"},"ReturnData":false}, {"Id":"ad1","Expression":"ANOMALY_DETECTION_BAND(m1)","ReturnData":true}]' \
  --evaluation-periods 1 \
  --alarm-actions
Allow the detector to learn for several days if possible. Use longer periods for metrics with slow cycles and shorter periods for rapid telemetry.
Testing checklist
  • Verify detector shows a learned band in the console graphs.
  • Simulate realistic load and confirm alarm only fires on genuine deviations.
  • Adjust sensitivity or evaluation periods if you see too many or too few alerts.
Common Mistake

Expecting immediate accurate detection. The model needs history and time to converge; test only after the band stabilizes.

screens.title: Composite Alarms — Reduce noise with logic
screens.subtitle: Combine multiple alarm states into a single, higher-level alarm

narration.text: Composite alarms allow you to combine the states of multiple CloudWatch child alarms using logical operators like AND, OR, and NOT. This is useful when no single metric indicates system failure, but a combination of signals does. For example, high C P U alone might be harmless, and low disk alone might be manageable, but when C P U is high and disk is low at the same time it may indicate an urgent capacity issue. Composite alarms evaluate the states of existing alarms and only change state when the rule expression is satisfied. A common misconception is thinking composite alarms replace the child alarms; they do not. Child alarms still exist and can be used independently; the composite alarm provides a higher-level abstraction for escalation. When designing composite alarms, keep expressions readable and name child alarms clearly so you can understand the composite condition during an incident. Also test by toggling child alarms into ALARM states to validate the composite behavior. What combination of signals in your environment would justify a composite alarm? Composite Alarms — Reduce noise with logic means use composite alarms to detect multi-signal failures and avoid acting on a single noisy metric.. In practical terms, combine multiple alarm states into a single, higher-level alarm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Combine signals, reduce noise
keyIdea.text: Use composite alarms to detect multi-signal failures and avoid acting on a single noisy metric.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Composite Alarms
Why composite alarms?
They reduce alert fatigue by escalating only when multiple conditions indicate a real problem.
Design tips:
  • Use clear child alarm names that describe the underlying condition.
  • Keep composite expressions simple: ALARM(A) AND ALARM(B) is more maintainable than nested complex logic.
  • Document the reason for the composite so on-call responders understand why it exists.
Example

Combine CPU high, disk low, and memory high in a composite alarm to only escalate when the host is genuinely degraded.

Implementation note
Composite alarms reference existing alarm ARNs and evaluate their states. They cannot directly reference metrics; use the child alarm objects to represent metric logic.
Common Mistake
Overly complex expressions that make debugging hard during incidents. Favor multiple, well-named composites over a single unreadable one.

screens.title: Amazon EventBridge — The event router
screens.subtitle: Match alarm events with patterns and send them to flexible targets

narration.text: EventBridge is a serverless event bus that accepts events from AWS services, your applications, and integrated SaaS providers, and routes them to many possible targets. For incident automation you commonly receive CloudWatch alarm state change events and then route them to Lambda, Step Functions, SQS, Kinesis, other event buses, or cross-account targets. The power of EventBridge lies in precise event patterns — JSON objects that match keys and values in an event payload to decide whether a rule triggers. A practical example: match events whose source is aws. cloudwatch, detail-type is CloudWatch Alarm State Change, and whose detail. alarmName equals your anomaly alarm, then invoke a Lambda that formats and posts a message to Slack and opens a ticket. A frequent error is creating overly broad patterns that fire for many alarms. Conversely, too specific patterns can miss events. Use the console's test feature and sample events to refine patterns. Think about enrichment and idempotency in targets; event-driven systems often retry or receive duplicates, so design idempotent handlers. Amazon EventBridge — The event router means author precise event patterns to match relevant alarms and send them to scalable targets for enrichment and remediation.. In practical terms, match alarm events with patterns and send them to flexible targets. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: EventBridge routes with precision
keyIdea.text: Author precise event patterns to match relevant alarms and send them to scalable targets for enrichment and remediation.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › EventBridge Basics
What EventBridge does
It matches incoming events to rules and routes them to one or more targets for processing or storage.
Design considerations:
  • Craft event patterns that are neither too broad nor too specific.
  • Use input transformers or a Lambda for enrichment before downstream systems.
  • Consider cross-account and cross-region routing for centralized incident telemetry.
Example event pattern
{
  "source": ["aws.cloudwatch"],
  "detail-type": ["CloudWatch Alarm State Change"],
  "detail": { "alarmName": ["High-CPU-Webserver-Alarm"], "state": { "value": ["ALARM"] } }
}
This pattern targets a single alarm name and state. Broaden or constrain fields depending on your routing needs.
Best practice
Test patterns using sample events and the console's test feature. Use input transformers to reduce the payload size sent to simple targets like SNS.

screens.title: EventBridge Rule to Lambda — Build the workflow
screens.subtitle: Route anomaly alarm events to a Lambda that enriches and forwards

narration.text: This lesson walks through designing an EventBridge rule that routes a CloudWatch alarm state change for an anomaly alarm to a Lambda for enrichment. The rule's event pattern matches events where the source is aws. cloudwatch and the detail-type is CloudWatch Alarm State Change, with the alarmName equal to your anomaly alarm and state value of ALARM. The target is a Lambda that logs the event, enriches it with runbook links and instance metadata, and then posts to a notification channel or opens a ticket. When you create the Lambda, grant EventBridge invoke permission and design the handler to be idempotent because events may be retried. Use input transformers when you only need a subset of fields to reduce downstream parsing. Test by triggering the alarm and watching CloudWatch Logs for Lambda execution and the EventBridge metrics for matched events. In complex scenarios, chain a Step Functions state machine as a target for multi-step automation that requires branching or waits. EventBridge Rule to Lambda — Build the workflow means eventbridge rules match alarm events and deliver them to targets that perform enrichment and orchestration.. In practical terms, route anomaly alarm events to a lambda that enriches and forwards. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Rule → Target → Enrichment
keyIdea.text: EventBridge rules match alarm events and deliver them to targets that perform enrichment and orchestration.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › EventBridge → Lambda
Design the rule
Match CloudWatch alarm state change events for a specific alarm and route to a Lambda target that enriches and forwards events.
Important elements:
  • Precise event pattern to avoid noisy matches.
  • Target Lambda with proper invoke permission.
  • Input transformer to send only necessary fields if desired.
Lambda example (Python)
def lambda_handler(event, context):
    # Log and enrich the incoming EventBridge event
    print("Received event:")
    print(event)
    # Example enrichment: add runbook link and instance metadata
    enriched = {
        'alarm': event.get('detail', {}).get('alarmName'),
        'state': event.get('detail', {}).get('state', {}).get('value'),
        'runbook': 'https://runbooks.example.com/incident-123'
    }
    print('Enriched event:', enriched)
    return {'statusCode': 200, 'body': 'Enriched event processed'}
Keep the handler idempotent and small. For complex orchestration use Step Functions as the target instead of embedding long pipelines in a single Lambda.

screens.title: Event Routes & Targets — Patterns for automation
screens.subtitle: Common target patterns and orchestration choices

narration.text: When routing alarm events, choose targets and patterns that fit the complexity of the response. For simple notifications and enrichment, EventBridge → Lambda → SNS or Slack is common. For multi-step remediation or approval flows, EventBridge → Step Functions provides durability and branching. If you need reliable queued processing, route to SQS or Kinesis and have workers consume and act asynchronously. For cross-account or multi-region observability, route alarms to a central event bus that fans out to analysis and pager systems. Consider idempotency: targets must handle duplicate or retried events safely. Another important design choice is enrichment placement. Enriching in a Lambda close to the event simplifies downstream systems, but adding enrichment later in the pipeline allows you to capture raw events centrally and defer interpretation. A practical example: route a C P U anomaly event to a Lambda that annotates the alarm with instance tags and then pushes to a ticketing system, while also sending the raw event to a central bus for long-term analytics. Think about observability, retries, and permissions when you choose the pattern. Event Routes & Targets — Patterns for automation means select targets—lambda, step functions, sqs—based on orchestration complexity, durability, and idempotency requirements.. In practical terms, common target patterns and orchestration choices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Match patterns to operational needs
keyIdea.text: Select targets—Lambda, Step Functions, SQS—based on orchestration complexity, durability, and idempotency requirements.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Event Targets
Lambda — Enrich & Notify
Use for lightweight enrichment, transformations, and direct API calls to ticketing or chat systems.
Step Functions — Orchestration
Use for multi-step remediation, waits, approvals, and retries with visible state history.
SQS / Kinesis — Durable queues
Route events to queues when you need reliable, backpressure-friendly processing at scale.
Concrete pattern
EventBridge receives CloudWatch alarm events, a Lambda enriches and formats them, Step Functions handles escalation with multiple steps, and SQS ensures reliable retries for long-running workers.
Operational reminder

Always grant least privilege to EventBridge and targets, and design handlers to be idempotent because events may be delivered more than once.

screens.title: Alarm Actions: Direct vs EventBridge
screens.subtitle: When to use CloudWatch alarm actions vs routing through EventBridge

narration.text: CloudWatch alarms can directly invoke actions like SNS topics, Auto Scaling, or EC2 actions. EventBridge adds flexibility by routing alarm events through a rule engine to many targets and enabling enrichment and orchestration. Use direct alarm actions when the response is simple and static, for example sending a pager notification via SNS for a single critical alarm. Choose EventBridge when you need to orchestrate a sequence of actions, enrich events, route differently based on content, or integrate with Step Functions and cross-account buses. A misconception is that EventBridge always adds latency or complexity; while it does add a routing layer, it often simplifies long-term automation by centralizing patterns and avoiding per-alarm Lambdas. Consider maintainability: if many alarms need the same enrichment and routing, create a single EventBridge rule and target rather than duplicating alarm actions. An example hybrid pattern is to have a CloudWatch alarm push to SNS for immediate paging but also emit an event to EventBridge for longer analysis and ticketing. Alarm Actions: Direct vs EventBridge means pick direct alarm actions for fast, single-step responses and eventbridge when you need flexible, testable workflows.. In practical terms, when to use cloudwatch alarm actions vs routing through eventbridge. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Direct actions for simple responses; EventBridge for orchestration
keyIdea.text: Pick direct alarm actions for fast, single-step responses and EventBridge when you need flexible, testable workflows.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Direct Actions vs EventBridge
Direct CloudWatch Actions
Attach SNS, Auto Scaling, or EC2 actions directly to an alarm for immediate, simple responses.
Pros and cons:
  • Fast and straightforward to configure.
  • Limited orchestration and enrichment capabilities.
EventBridge Routing
Use for flexible patterns, enrichment, multi-target routing, and complex automation workflows.
Pros and cons:
  • Centralizes automation patterns and supports many targets.
  • Requires designing event patterns and targets, slightly more upfront work.
Example hybrid

Send immediate pager notifications via SNS for critical alarms while also emitting an EventBridge event for enrichment, ticketing, and analysis.

screens.title: Naming, Thresholds, and Event Pattern Tips
screens.subtitle: Practical rules to keep detection reliable and maintainable

narration.text: This lesson collects best practices for naming, thresholding, and crafting event patterns so your detection landscape remains maintainable. Start with descriptive names that include component, metric, and intent, for example MyService-A P I-ErrorRate-Alarm. Use consistent namespaces and dimensions so metric math expressions and alarms are easier to construct and reuse. For thresholds, prefer derived metrics and anomaly detection for fluctuating telemetry; reserve static thresholds for well-known limits like disk capacity percentages. For event patterns, prefer matching on structured fields like detail-type and alarmName or namespace rather than inspecting free-form messages. A frequent operational pitfall is overly narrow patterns keyed to ephemeral identifiers; use tags or standardized labels to group alarms. Document the owner and runbook URL in alarm descriptions or include them in enriched EventBridge payloads so responders have immediate context. Finally, include tests in your deployment process: simulate alarms, verify EventBridge rules match, and confirm targets receive and handle events as expected. screens.subtitle: Three core ideas to carry forward

narration.text: Summarizing the chapter, remember three core ideas. First, metric math turns raw telemetry into meaningful signals like error rates, which are less sensitive to traffic volume. Second, anomaly detection provides adaptive bands so metrics with seasonal or cyclic patterns alert only when they truly diverge from normal behavior. Third, EventBridge acts as a flexible router that matches alarm state-change events via JSON patterns and forwards them to targets such as Lambda, Step Functions, SQS, or other event buses for enrichment and automation. Keep these concepts in mind when designing detection: derive stable signals, avoid static thresholds on fluctuating metrics, and centralize routing where you need orchestration.
